prompt_text:
This figure gives an overview of therapeutic strategies for intestinal barrier dysfunction and immune dysregulation, likely in inflammatory bowel disease or related monogenic disorders. It organizes treatments by the biological level they target: the intestinal barrier, innate immune cells, adaptive lymphocytes, and cellular therapies.

At the barrier level, the diagram highlights epithelial, mesenchymal, and endothelial components, with drugs such as mesalazine, losartan, and eculizumab acting on pathways involving cyclooxygenase/PPARγ, TGFβ signaling, and complement activation. The central portion focuses on phagocytes and inflammatory signaling. It shows bacterial sensing pathways, IL-10 signaling, mTOR, and inflammasome-related mechanisms, with multiple targeted agents blocking cytokines such as IL-6, TNF, IL-12/23, IL-1, and IL-18, or modulating pathways like NLRP3 and NLRC4.

The lower section summarizes lymphocyte-directed therapies. Naive CD4 T cells are shown differentiating into several helper subsets and FOXP3-positive regulatory cells, while treatments interfere with co-stimulation, IL-2 signaling, T-cell receptor signaling, JAK-STAT pathways, gut homing via α4β7 integrin, and DNA/RNA synthesis. On the far right, cellular therapies include allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and gene-corrected patient stem cells, both aiming to restore functional immune cell populations.
